title: Advent at home
hook: a wreath, a Jesse tree, quiet evenings
tomorrow: so when does Christmas actually end?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the stranger in the back pew: the door is wide. Today the door is your own front door, and the question is what happens behind it in December.
screen: `THE DOOR IS WIDE.` → `YOUR OWN FRONT DOOR.`

segments.voice: The neighbors' lights went up the weekend after Thanksgiving. The radio has been playing carols for weeks. And in some Catholic homes, the tree stays in the garage until Christmas Eve, and the house is quiet, with purple candles, for four weeks. In other Catholic homes, the tree goes up early and the waiting happens with the lights on. Same Church, same season, two very different living rooms. Both families have their reasons, and both reasons are worth hearing.
screen: `LIGHTS UP AFTER THANKSGIVING.` → `TREE IN THE GARAGE TILL CHRISTMAS EVE.` → `TWO LIVING ROOMS.`

segments.voice: The Church's own description gives both sides something. Its norms for the liturgical year say Advent has two faces: getting ready for Christmas, when Christ's first coming is remembered, and turning minds toward his coming at the end of time. And they call it a season of devout and joyful expectation. View one, the quiet house. Advent is its own season, not early Christmas. A wreath with four candles, one more lit each week. A Jesse tree, hung with small ornaments for the people who waited through the Old Testament: Adam, Noah, Abraham, David. Advent hymns, like O come, O come, Emmanuel, with the carols saved for later. Its best case: if you feast for a month first, Christmas Day arrives tired. The waiting is what makes the joy land. View two, the early tree. Joyful expectation is still joy. Lights in the darkest stretch of the year are a sign of what's coming, and a family decorating together on a December night is already waiting together. Its best case: a home isn't a church, and kids learn a season by living inside it. Here's one to tell a friend tonight: the third Sunday of Advent is called Gaudete, Latin for rejoice, from Paul's line to rejoice in the Lord always. On the wreath, its candle is often rose, not purple. Even the quiet house has a day when the joy breaks in early.
screen: `DEVOUT AND JOYFUL EXPECTATION.` · `THE QUIET HOUSE: WAITING MAKES JOY LAND.` · `THE EARLY TREE: JOY THAT WAITS.` · `GAUDETE: REJOICE.` · then, large: `WAIT AT HOME.`

segments.voice: Make a small Advent plan in three steps. First the wish: one thing you'd want your December evenings to hold, a candle at dinner, ten quiet minutes, a carol saved for Christmas. Then the obstacle that will get in its way, the schedule, the phone, being tired, and the plan: when that happens, what you'll do instead. Hold that one sentence for the rest of the sit.
Advent at home. Waiting for Christmas in your own house: a wreath, a Jesse tree, quiet evenings, lights on or off.
Your line: wait at home. Both houses in the debate are waiting, one with the lights off, one with them on. See you tomorrow.
